📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just a small warning: There is one spoiler below (about the fate of the dog) for Heart of the Beast, but that’s the only spoiler. If you want to know his fate before watching this, I understand, so I’ve included it here.

In a recent development, amid all the talk about potential Oscar movies, one film that I actually loved on the 2026 movie schedule that isn’t really getting a lot of attention is Heart of the Beast, starring Brad Pitt. Pitt plays Sergeant Major James Belmont, a retired Special Forces operator, and four different dogs play his trusty companion and fellow war vet, Odin. If you’re wondering, because I know I was, Odin does not die in the movie, so you can rest easy on that front. What Odin does do, along with Pitt, is help deliver a wonderful, heartfelt story that I really want everyone to see.

According to recent reports, the story, at its most basic, is a survival one. Belmont and Odin find themselves stranded in the Alaskan bush and must hike miles through the unforgiving wilderness. Really, though, it’s about a man and his dog and what they do for each other, in good times and bad, that the movie is really about. It’s as touching a movie about a friendship as has ever been. Their bond is real, and it is felt from beginning to end.

Industry observers note that it isn’t an easy movie to watch, and there are some brutal and intense moments of survival and some carnage to endure. It makes the end so worth it, as the audience, like Belmont, is exhausted. In fact, the moments at the end, some of the most heartbreaking in the movie, come with both sadness and relief after the duo endures to survive. I’m an unabashed Brad Pitt fan, and I think this is some of his best work. It’s also very different from what we often expect from the actor. There is no “coolness” to his character, but there is real strength.

In full transparency, walking into the theater for my screening, I was not looking forward to watching Heart of the Beast. I really debated whether I wanted to see it. Setting aside the possible fate of the dog, I just didn’t know if I wanted to sit through a survival movie, knowing what was sure to come. And I won’t lie, there are some moments I really struggled to watch. I’m not particularly squeamish, but one scene in particular hit way too close to home, and it was tough.

Sources indicate that however, it’s worth it! I promise it is. When the lights came up at the end and I started thinking about all that had happened in the movie, it was immensely satisfying. So much so that I really was rooting for it to be a sleeper hit. It wasn’t a huge hit, but it did end up earning just under $200 million over its run at the box office, where it did steady, if not spectacular, business over a few weeks. While Pitt's other movie this year, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, is getting rave early reviews, I hope it doesn't totally overshadow this one.

Sources indicate that heart of the Beast is at the moment available to buy or rent on VOD, and I urge you to take a chance on it. I think you’ll be surprised just how good it is.

Unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that strategy release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the firm has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental complications.

According to recent reports, unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

The grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

In a recent development, the manifesto states that "GenAI is right now harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people.".

The manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture.".

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the manufacturer code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games.".

It has been revealed that it's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that my greatest regret about Grand Theft Auto 6's release is that I didn't make an 'angry players' bingo card beforehand. Seriously, with how predictable all the outrage is, I could've had the winning card by now, and the game's not even been out for 24 hours yet.

What would I have on my bingo card? Well, a couple of things that'd be on there are: angry at 30 fps, angry at shooting police (a classic), and slap-bang in the middle I'd have angry that you can't cheat (the other kind of cheat) on your partner.

It seems that there's a group of players who are taking issue with the fact that GTA 6's story revolves around Jason and Lucia's relationship and therefore you can't pick up other women like strippers or Mandy, an early side character who players seem to be quite preoccupied with right now. Although, I haven't heard anyone complain that Lucia can't get with other guys.

You can still go to strip clubs, though. You can even go as a couple; how modern. But Rockstar hasn't added the ability to do much more simply because it doesn't fit with the story. In a statement to Shacknews Rockstar explains:.

Industry observers note that "GTA 6 is a game about a couple in a bind, lovers on the run. While we have taken a lot forward from previous GTA titles, everything we have implemented in [GTA 6] has been done to support the spirit of the story we wanted to tell, and the gameplay systems we wanted to expand upon—things like the wanted system, the radio, robberies and car theft. Many aspects of previous titles are not present in GTA 6, but the elements we have we believe are all necessary and complementary to the feeling and motivations we wanted to emphasise as you play through Jason and Lucia's story.".

In a recent development, honestly, it makes sense. Given the fact that this story clearly revolves around the two of them you'd probably have a considerably worse time towards the end if there was an option to break the couple up. It's bad enough running into your ex in public, but imagine having to do a bank heist with them? Yeah, no thanks.

Recent findings suggest that I'm sure once (or whenever) GTA 6 online comes out players will be able to do whatever they please. But for now you'll have to stay within the confine of GTA 6's storylines, which means being in a loving relationship, how sad.

Rainbow Six now sits under Vantage Studios, the Ubisoft subsidiary set up last year that also oversees Assassin’s Creed and Far Cry, and in which Tencent holds a 26.32 percent stake.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All GTA 6 pre-orders come with a free month of GTA+, which nets you some in-game bonuses like a free vehicle, garage, and higher selling prices.

But before you excitedly claim your freebie, it’s essential you understand auto-renew will be enabled.

This means unless you disable it, you’ll be charged the monthly price of $7.99/£6.99/€7.99 as soon as your free month is over.

Once you’ve claimed your free trial, from the PS5’s home screen scroll left to the PS Store and select ‘...’ > Subscriptions:.

You’ll see all of your active subscriptions listed.

Select ‘GTA+’ and press ‘Cancel Subscription’:.

Don’t worry, you’ll still get to enjoy the entirety of your free month, this will just prevent you from being charged.

If you want to keep GTA+, then of course you don’t need to do this. Just be aware you will get charged every month. You can also re-activate your subscription if you choose to do so by repeating the steps above:.

Hopefully this heads-up helps anyway.

To be fair, the PS5 does tell you about this when activating your free month, but it’s GTA 6 release day and I suspect some of you will be giddy and not necessarily in the mood for the fine print.

In a recent development, if you want to play GTA 6 natively on any console right now, you can only do so on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S or PS5. However, if you're willing to use the cloud, it's possible to play the game on Xbox One.

To do this, you have to buy the game on the Xbox Store first, and then acquire Xbox Cloud Gaming time via one of two means - you either purchase time on the Xbox Store, or you get a subscription to Xbox Game Pass that includes a certain amount of time per-tier (and you can top it up later if you need to).

Here's the breakdown for all of those:.

There is also the option to play "free with ads" using Xbox Cloud Gaming, but we haven't verified that it works with GTA 6 yet (although there's seemingly no reason why it wouldn't), and it only gives you 30 minutes of game time before it kicks you off. Some of GTA 6's missions can last longer than 30 minutes, so that's not really ideal.

Anyway, while we're still in the process of dusting off our Xbox One consoles and trying GTA 6 on there for ourselves, we thought we'd first share some impressions from Xbox fans across the web on what it's been like for them so far.

Let's take a look at what some Xbox One owners are saying about it:.

Overall, it seems like most people are enjoying their time with GTA 6 on Xbox One so far, although that's not to say there haven't been challenges in some cases. The biggest complaints seem to be that some players think it looks "blurry" (while others don't really see a problem), and there are also a small number of reports that it appears to disconnect for no reason sometimes.

There's also a bit of worry that the servers might not be able to handle the load during "peak" hours, and considering we're only on the first day of GTA 6's official launch, it's hard to say how things are going to go in that regard.

Meanwhile, every other version of Xbox Cloud Gaming officially runs at up to 1080p and 12mbps bitrate.

According to recent reports, if you want any further feedback about playing GTA 6 on the Xbox One, we'll aim to get some "hands on" impressions to you ASAP. Based on these initial day one impressions though, it seems to be working fairly well right now.

Keep in mind that you obviously need a strong and consistent internet connection in order to play games via Xbox Cloud Gaming, otherwise you may experience heavy lag, disconnects and all sorts of other problems.

Sources indicate that are you playing GTA 6 on Xbox One? Please let us know your impressions of it in the comments below!

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, which is available with a Hulu subscription, was an instant sensation. It shone a spotlight on the success and scandals of its O.G. cast, including the drama prone Taylor Frankie Paul. Because of that attention, it felt like a given that producers would want to do a spinoff, which led to the recent debut of an Orange County, Calif. version centered around Jen Affleck on the 2026 TV schedule.

The newly introduced series has a mix of faith-based Mormons alongside women who either seem to be taking a break from the Church or just don’t want anything to do with it at all, which of course is going to lead to some friction. When clashes escalate, viewers can’t help but notice, and executive producer Jeff Jenkins got worried that the cast might not make it through the season. He told The Wrap that while they ended the season in a better place, it was questionable for a minute:.

There’s still friggin’ potholes of disagreement, but I think they end stronger as a group than when they began. I didn’t even know if they were going to make it through week one. Honestly, I was like, ‘Oh my god, these girls are going to murder each other.’.

Recent findings suggest that he's likely joking about the whole "murder" thing, but having seen the Hulu reality series, I get where the sentiment comes from. The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County is comprised of two groups that former Dancing with the Stars contestant Affleck wants to bring together – the “Molly Mormons,” who are all-in on their faith, and the “Jack Mormons,” who either more loosely follow the teachings or have left it behind entirely. That can be a challenge in any setting, so it was not surprising when the tension between Mayci Neeley’s older sister McCall DePron and internet personality Bobbi Althoff became more heated.

The good news is that the Mormon Wives: OC cast genuinely does seem to have ended in a better place than they started, and no murder has actually been committed. When you’re just getting to know each other and feeling out what someone’s boundaries are, clashes are bound to happen, especially when you have some different viewpoints and perspectives. It’s what you do once you know a person better that matters. And Bobbi even publicly posted on Instagram Stories to ask people to stop bullying McCall, as they worked out their own differences. Here’s what she had to say, in her own words:.

A post shared by The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives News & Updates (@secretlivesupdates).

Industry observers note that largely because of Taylor Frankie Paul, the original The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives series has had its fair share of chaos surrounding production. After the cancellation of her season of The Bachelorette and custody concerns with her children, the MomTok star announced that she was leaving the show. Things haven’t gone that far with anyone in the Orange County spinoff.

Sure, they have some personal drama, from Jen Affleck deciding she wants to follow through with a divorce while pregnant with her fourth child, and Aspyn Ovard publicly showing what her life is like as part of a throuple. Bobbi even admitted to signing on for the heightened visibility reality TV brings. They also seem to genuinely want to be there as a support system for Jen and are willing to give each other grace through the mistakes and missteps.

While waiting to hear about whether there will be a Season 2 for the Orange County cast and the status of the original series seems a bit unclear, fellow Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt is getting her own reality show. It will certainly be interesting to see how things play out for all of these women, and hopefully they will continue to not murder each other.

I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again.
  • Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did.
  • According to recent reports, for Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that big a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in Fresh York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

According to recent reports, for Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

Sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Recent findings suggest that then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

In a recent development, you could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

Recent findings suggest that they often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

According to recent reports, the latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

Recent findings suggest that they aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Harder to upgrade if you aren't well-versed in back-connect motherboards.
  • Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The revamped version of the Maingear Zero feels even more bespoke to its cable-less design philosophy. With a homemade case and cooler from Maingear itself, the Mk.2 doubles down on what made this PC great to begin with. It's a gaming desktop that emphasises this brand's pristine build quality, and one that will be an absolute showstopper to have in your setup. It comes at a premium though, and not just because of the RAMpocalypse.

Harder to upgrade if you aren't well-versed in back-connect motherboards.

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

According to recent reports, 2026 is a dreadful time to be shopping for a new desktop PC. I know that; you probably all know that, and PC hardware brands who are struggling to shift any new products due to massive price inflations definitely know that. For many, the current economy means upgrading is written off entirely, because the expense is just too high at the moment. But when the going gets tough, the tough get going, and Maingear's latest attempt to reinstate itself as the best gaming PC builder embodies that.

It has been revealed that it seems to me that Maingear understands the following; if gamers are going to upgrade their PC at the moment, it might as well be for a good reason. In other words, the products on offer need to be flawless to entice people to buy them because they really need to be worth the added expense they bring. When I reviewed the first rendition of the Maingear Zero Ruby back in 2024, I already thought it was worth its premium price tag, not just because the computer itself was beautiful, but because this brand makes a point of going the extra mile with its products on behalf of its customers.

Back then, the Zero's concept was novel - it was the first range of prebuilt PCs to use back-connect motherboards. But at some point in 2025, the Zero range quietly disappeared from Maingear's store, only seeing a revival this year alongside the revamped MG-1 flagship the brand prides itself on. This Mk.2 rendition of the Zero is going to cost you more than the original ever did, but it makes modern enhancements that would tempt any PC gamer into ignoring the RAMpocalypse and slapping their money down on the table.

I mean, just look at this thing. The panoramic glass, the multi-angle AIO cooler display, the seven pre-installed fans, the absolutely spotless build quality? It takes the novel idea of a PC with zero visible cables we saw two years ago and takes it to the next level.

Industry observers note that case in point, this PC was actually really difficult to take review photos of because its fancy, futuristic glass meant no matter the angle I snapped from, I'd be somewhere in the reflection. That's an annoyance for me, but a very, very good thing for you because this is the sort of PC that displays your components beautifully, and something you'll want on display as the heart of your gaming setup. Don't put this thing under your desk - it's something to show off.

Recent findings suggest that I went to Computex this year; I've seen some innovations in fans, I've seen new case designs that look fancy and futuristic, and I've seen mice with upward-firing fans in them. But I think the Zero Mk.2 might be the best-looking bit of gaming PC hardware I've seen this year. The adoption of panoramic glass is huge, but the way it works in tandem with a cooler that's visible from every angle takes the clean, cableless design philosophy to new heights. It also manages to look bigger on the inside than it actually is, but more on that in a minute.

It has been revealed that first, we have to talk about the build quality - which I shouldn't be surprised by, knowing Maingear as a brand, but I still was. There are often nitpicks I have with prebuilt gaming PCs when I review them. For example, the GPU bracket Quoted Tech chose in the PC they sent was blatantly wrong, causing friction with an intake fan and making an annoying whirring sound. Especially having built and rebuilt my own PCs for years now, these things can be easy to spot. But I went through the Maingear Zero Mk.2 with a fine-toothed comb; there's nothing to pick apart. In the box, there's even a checklist to evidence the PC you've received has been built to high standards and stress-tested before it even gets to you. This time around, I even saw improvements on the first Zero.

According to recent reports, the annoying GPU support bracket from the original was so integrated into the motherboard that even to add a newly introduced SSD in, you had to disassemble the entire graphics card and faceplate first. This has been improved so it's more practical this time around.

Something else that I love is that Maingear has opted for a pretty reasonably sized chassis for the revamped Zero. As far as I'm aware, it's Maingear's own, homemade Zero Mk.2 case, which wasn't the case last time, as MSI's MAG Pano M100 PZ was borrowed for it - presumably as part of whatever deal was struck to get hold of the brand's motherboards.

This time around, Maingear has taken a lot of design notes from Cooler Master, MSI, Asus, and now NZXT with their curved-glass PC cases. But the actual physical size of this chassis is a compact mATX that fits ATX boards. It means the PC can be a reasonable size that'll fit on top of your desk, in a showy position in your room, or in a tighter space in a smaller gaming room.

In a recent development, when the first batch of Zero PCs hit the shelves, these motherboards were still relatively new on the scene; they were quirky and were harder to come by. Now, their concept isn't so novel, and there's a larger range of boards, including smaller mATX ones that help Maingear to keep things compact here.

It has been revealed that of course, one downside in grabbing a PC like this with a back-connect motherboard is that maintaining that pristine look over the years might make things difficult. If you want to upgrade one of these rigs but you're not that sure of how to perform various PC surgeries, the advice you find online will only be harder to follow if you take on a motherboard that isn't conventional. Furthermore, it's going to be very difficult not to disrupt Maingear's very neat and tidy PC assembly job when you upgrade, so it feels like there would be a risk of messing things up if you go to upgrade your machine later. That's just something to think about.

In a recent development, as you can see, the ceiling for the new range of Zero PCs is a bit ludicrous, with the Amethyst configuration (which is the closest comparison to my review unit) costing $7,299 at the time of writing. Yes, you did read that right.

Some interesting disparities between the version I tested and what you'll get are that, while I had a B860 chipset for an AMD processor, you can have either an AMD CPU for gaming or an Intel Core Ultra 200S Plus one - this is one of the few pre-built PCs outside of custom builds that allow you to configure either an AMD or Intel chipset.

Also interesting is that I had XPG RAM, while all the other versions of the Zero Mk.2 are advertised to have Kingston Fury memory in them. I don't imagine the reason I was sent something different was anything to do with hiding the performance you'll get - it's probably much more likely that Maingear was using whatever it had stock of for my temporary review unit.

Alongside this top-of-the-range configuration though, the Zero Mk.2 comes in an "Elite" version harnessing an RTX 5080. Right now, all of the named, prebuilt variations of the newly introduced Ruby are sold out, but you can still fully customize one to be built to your exact specifications. From what I gather on Maingear's builder, the Zero starts at $2,988, with minimum component options being an 8GB RTX 5060 Ti, AMD Ryzen 5 9600X, 32GB of RAM, and 2TB SSD.

If you do want to spare yourself some expense, Maingear does have a BYO-RAM option which might help to take that minimum spend down a touch. Funnily enough, I remember criticising the configurations of the original Maingear Zero for so many of them only offering 16GB of DDR5 despite their high prices. Now, during RAMageddon, the minimum this sequel PC comes with is 32GB.

I guess I'm sorry for saying anything.

As is always the case when I'm supplied with a review unit that spares absolutely no expense when it comes to power, these performance figures are going to be relevant to you only if you opt for a 5090 configuration. Do not expect these kinds of numbers if you opt for the more affordable 5060 Ti versions of this machine. Still, I'm always going to put a review model through its paces, and I was particularly keen to see if aesthetically flawless building amounted to strong performance.

The GPU being an RTX 5090, I can happily say that no PSU cables spontaneously combusted during this review - I'd love to say this is a solid sign that thermals are being handled well by the newly introduced Maingear Zero Mk.2 case, but that may just be luck of the draw with the GPU, PSU, and its cables.

According to recent reports, on that note, the GPU was actually warmer during my testing than the CPU, with the Ryzen 7 only peaking at 69 degrees Celsius during 3DMark's Time Spy benchmark, while the RTX 5090 reached 73 degrees. Elsewhere in benchmarking the CPU had higher peaks, but the GPU had higher mean temperatures overall, which tells you a lot about the 5090. At the same time, credit where it's due goes to the Maingear 360mm AIO cooler, which kept the beefy X3D processor cool under strenuous workloads.

Cinebench:Multi Thread: 5605ptsSingle Core: 761ptsSingle Thread: 562pts.

3DMark:TimeSpy: 36,896Firestrike: 66,029Steel Nomad: 140.94fps.

CrystalDiskMark:Sequential read: 7,387 MB/sSequential write: 6,769 MB/s.

AIDA64 Extreme / RAM readings:59,228 MB/s read30-36-36-76 (6,000MT/s).

One thing I'd like to point out is that, just like the original Maingear Zero, something that really stands out about this brand's computers is that they buck the trend of most PC builders by supplying some really top-rate RAM and SSDs. Usually, this is where pre-build companies make a bit of money back because they'll give you the headline GPU and CPU specs you want, but the quality of the RAM and SSDs will be lesser because they don't matter quite so much. Maingear's attitude is a little different, because it wants to give you nothing but the best parts, and it reveals in testing.

The SSD here achieved a 7,000+MB/s read speed, which is what you'd hope for when it comes to a Gen 4 NVMe M.2 SSD - a lot of the time PCs can house SSDs that get stuck in the 5,000s, which is okay, but not great for the money you pay for one of these Zero Mk.2 rigs. At a time like this, when SSDs and RAM will be harder to come by and cost you more, that could be a good or a bad thing, but at least you know you're getting quality parts here - perhaps more affordably than if you were to buy separately due to Maingear likely buying in bulk and having partnerships with suppliers like TeamGroup.

I'd love to applaud the fact that the RAM aboard the Zero Mk.2 achieved a higher AIDA Extreme reading than desktops I've tested previously, but since it's not the standard memory from Kingston you'll receive in your machine, it may not matter so much. If you choose to bring your own RAM to the Zero Mk.2, the benchmarks above will at least show you what's possible.

It's no surprise at all that, seeing as this is actually the first 5090 rig I've reviewed so far this generation, the gaming and software benchmarks are the highest you'll see in any chart.

The RTX 5090 is a ridiculous piece of kit, but even before the RAMpocalypse, it was always priced out of reach of the majority of gamers. Even to begin with, I don't think the RTX 5090 was really designed for gamers anyway, and it was mainly designed, as the 4090 was, for AI consumers, crypto mining, pro-level 3D artists, and content creators. Keep that in mind while looking at the benchmarks here. They're absurdly powerful, but probably not what most gamers will actually need when buying even a premium-level PC, especially when one like this will presently cost you more than a car.

There's a hell of a combination of parts coming together to work in tandem in these results, and like I say, there's no surprise the Zero Mk.2 has recorded the highest results of any PC I've ever benchmarked.

It'd be easy for me to draw the line there and say, since it's the most powerful PC, it's the best overall, but that'd actually be cutting the Maingear Zero Mk.2 short.

There's more to actually using this PC than its parts that I think makes it the best, and after all, you might not have one with an RTX 5090 in it.

In a recent development, for example, thermals are really solid here, which can sometimes suffer in cases designed specifically to look good. Even under these stressful benchmarks, I don't think I really noticed the fans kicking up much of an audible fuss from under my desk once. The Zero Mk.2 is compact, it's quiet, and it's the most powerful and best-built PC I've come across. Again, the RTX 5090 configuration outguns even some of the other highest-end PCs I've benchmarked, but even with a 5080, I think the stronger supporting components here would mean the Zero Mk.2 could stand a chance at pulling ahead of the competition on performance.

Moreover, while you pay a premium for Maingear goods, you do get some of the best warranty, servicing, and customer service options I've seen from a PC building brand. Maingear PCs get lifetime service and repairs. Even if you pass the PC on to a friend or sell it on, the label and number on the back sticker of the PC means you can quote it to a service agent, and they'll be happy to help with whatever is wrong with the rig.

It has been revealed that and the PC that arrives with you has absolutely minimal bloatware other than what Windows insists you have. The sample I received was packaged well with an inner and outer box, expanding foam in case you need to send it back or pack it up during a house move; there are set-up instructions, and everything in the PC comes properly installed so that you don't need to do a thing to get going besides plug things in and get started.

Are this tech giant's PC's constantly in high demand, and do they cost a premium? Yes, and that might be your biggest barrier to entry.

The Maingear Zero Mk.2 has doubled down on what made the original my favorite gaming PC I've tested. It's somehow got an even cleaner build this time around, and its case and cooler only complement that, with a design that lets the cableless beauty within speak for itself.

Maingear has managed to design and execute something that lets you have the best of every world when it comes to buying a upcoming PC. There's a compact size here that makes it versatile for your setup and the way you want to use it. There's an option to cram it with some of the beefiest and best components out there, and it's all something that looks a million dollars without making itself heard due to poor thermals.

That stated, I do think this brand should be treated like the holy grail of the prebuilt market. The prices here are high, and yes, you're paying more than you would from other companies for an additional level of quality. But I wouldn't be doing my job if I didn't say there are other PC makers out there that won't charge quite as much and still give you the specs, an attractive design, and great thermals.

Industry observers note that I think the people who should be looking for a Maingear Zero Mk.2 are the ones who want an absolute showstopper of a PC that can do it all. For those prepared to spare no expense, there's no PC I'd recommend harder.

I put the Maingear Zero Mk.2 through its paces by using it for around 2 weeks. In that time, I put it through all of the formal benchmarking tests we here at GamesRadar+ use to recommend you new computing tech. I played games with it, I created some video content, and I put it through strict benchmarking tests in both the gaming and content creation software worlds. I kept track of data on frame rates, temperatures, and more.

I also evaluated pricing, tech specs, and Maingear as a brand to come to a verdict.

In a recent development, we are now just four days away from the release of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X/S and PS5, but the proximity to the much-anticipated launch date isn't stemming the tide of leaks that has been plaguing the game for much of the past year. Yesterday, a fresh video - seemingly from a record store that received vinyl records of the soundtrack early - demonstrated off the full 34-song tracklist for the game.

According to recent reports, thanks to the listing printed on the back of Grand Theft Auto 6: The Album vinyl, we have a better idea of the licensed music that'll appear in-game. Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson are just some of the names that make up the impressive list. We know about a few of these tracks from September's announcement of the record, but only six tracks were revealed then, not the whole list.

Take a look at the full track listing below:.

It has been revealed that you can expect to hear these tracks on the radio - alongside many more, no doubt - and deployed at curated times during cutscenes or in missions, to really tie together the vibe of the city. This is something Vice City did remarkably well its roster of 80s tracks, and I can't wait to see how Rockstar has used more contemporary music in the same way here.

Of course, there have been a lot of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks in the run-up to the game's launch. Another recent example is the full game's map which seemingly leaked online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store. Then there were all the leaks from a group calling itself CyberLeek, which shared unofficial gameplay and map details over the course of a few weeks, before Rockstar had even revealed much gameplay itself.

It has been revealed that amongst all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher Newly introduced Blood Interactive's latest upgrade post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

Sources indicate that in addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by Newly introduced Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

According to recent reports, other than these new hires, the enhancement is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

Industry observers note that the patch is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

You'll need to chase them down and do a bit of high-speed shooting. Recent findings suggest that as initially reported by Vertical Slice (thanks, Chris!), the workforce of Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics is being cut as part of a new set of layoffs by owners Embracer. As far as is right now known, those affected include senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, and UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, all of whom shared news of their redunancies on LinkedIn. There may be more affected, but neither Crystal Dynamics nor Embracer have offered comments on the reduction of staff as yet.

Industry observers note that according to Legacy of Atlantis' Steam page, generative AI has been used in the development of Legacy of Atlantis "to support some early exploration and temporary development content. Any AI-assisted assets were either replaced or refined by humans in order to maintain the creative and artistic vision of the development team." I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

  • It has been revealed that in a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope.
  • In a recent development, of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, blade Runner 2099 - an upcoming TV miniseries coming to Amazon Prime Video, acting as a sequel to Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) - might be getting a video game. And a 'triple-A' video game, at that. At least that's according to Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment (which owns the Blade Runner IP).

It has been revealed that in a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope. Other than that, the duo seemed to want to keep any potential information to themselves. Given they appear to be in talks about the title, rather than in any active development, if something did come of this ideation, it would no doubt be a long, long way off. Kosove and Johnson's aim seems to be getting players to "interact" more with the world of Blade Runner, which has recently been fleshed out by the 2017 movie and is set to be developed more in the upcoming series.

In a recent development, of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before. There was 1997's simply-titled Blade Runner - developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Interactive - which was a point-and-click adventure that really seemed to pick up the vibes the original Ridley Scott was putting down. An Enhanced Edition of the game was released in 2022, which is actually more of a remake than a simple enhancement.

Then, in 2023, Annapurna Interactive unveiled its very first internally-developed game, in the form of Blade Runner 2033: Labyrinth. The game, which promised to riff on the dystopian universe established in Ridley Scott's cult classic movie, would have been sandwiched squarely between that film and its sequel, Blade Runner 2049. It was going to be set in LA after the Blackout hits, but beyond that - and the fact it's coming to PC and consoles at some point - few details ever managed to break through the PR barrier before the game went dark: it's been removed from Annapurna's website and delisted from Steam. Curious.

If you want to see something more from the cyberpunk world sooner, Blade Runner 2099 releases on Prime Video on 25th November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As GTA 6 brings in rave reviews and – predictably – takes over the internet as millions of players dive into Rockstar's long-awaited blockbuster, industry veteran Peter Moore notes "the video game industry could really use a moment like this.".

It has been revealed that moore, who previously served as president of Sega of America, corporate vice president of Microsoft's home and entertainment division responsible for Xbox marketing and operations, and CEO of EA, has taken to Twitter in the wake of Rockstar's latest launch. First, he offers an AI-modified image of himself with a GTA 6 tattoo in place of his infamous GTA 4 tattoo, which was revealed at E3 2006 to confirm the game's simultaneous launch on Xbox 360 and PS3.

But "in all seriousness," he adds, GTA 6's launch is an vital one, and not just for the fans who've been waiting 13 years to play a upcoming Grand Theft Auto game.

According to recent reports, "We've been through a challenging period," he acknowledges. "Studio closures, redundancies, canceled projects and enormous uncertainty have taken their toll on an industry that has given so much to so many, myself included.

"That's why the launch of GTA VI feels so significant," he continues. "It's more than the release of a hugely anticipated game. It's an opportunity to remind the world of the extraordinary power of this industry to create, innovate, entertain and bring people together.".

As someone who's spent so much time in the games industry, Moore says, "I've seen this industry reinvent itself time and time again." With that in mind, he hopes GTA 6 is able to deliver "the commercial success we all expect, but perhaps more importantly, I hope it provides a much-needed shot in the arm (no pun intended…) for the entire ecosystem: developers, publishers, studios, retailers, technology partners and the next generation of creative talent." After all, he says, "The games industry has always been at its best when it dares to dream substantial.".

Well, as far as things go on the commercial front, it looks like the game has had an extremely strong start. Rockstar hasn't revealed any official figures, but with analysts' old launch week predictions going as high as $5.2 billion, and more recent estimates placing the revenue as of yesterday at $1.65 billion, it's safe that plenty of folks are buying it.

Breaking: Sony defeat $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit which argued PlayStation's dominant market position fuels "excessive and unfair" game prices

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (476 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony.
  • As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.
  • The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the tech giant of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

In a recent development, it's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

According to recent reports, in a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

In a recent development, as if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Recent findings suggest that every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another massive game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

GTA 6 Has an Easy Mode Buried in an Impressive Range of Accessibility Options

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 is easily the most customisable game that Rockstar has ever made when it comes to accessibility options.
  • Industry observers note that there's a wide range of settings and toggles to experiment with, in a bid to make the open world experience more comfortable.
  • But there are a couple of settings in particular that have raised eyebrows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is easily the most customisable game that Rockstar has ever made when it comes to accessibility options.

Industry observers note that there's a wide range of settings and toggles to experiment with, in a bid to make the open world experience more comfortable. And while the initiative isn't quite as in-depth as what you'll find in recent Ubisoft or Sony-published titles, it's still a solid step forward for the studio.

But there are a couple of settings in particular that have raised eyebrows. As you might know, Rockstar never deals in difficulty levels; outside of things like adjustable aim assist, you're always in line with the developer's intended challenge.

In GTA 6, however, there are two difficulty-related toggles buried in the accessibility options: 'Accessible Combat' and 'Reduced Vehicle Damage'.

In a recent development, in essence, both settings amount to having an easy mode. Accessible Combat decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider.

Meanwhile, Reduced Vehicle Damage does exactly what it says on the tin, making your chosen ride more durable.

But just how much easier do these toggles make GTA 6? The options menu itself concerns a warning, stating that when enabled, the "balance and experience" of the game is "significantly" changed.

We've put them to the test, and despite some claims I've seen floating around the internet this morning, they do not make you invincible. You still need to play the game as intended — actually taking cover in firefights, for example — but the overall level of challenge is still noticeably reduced.

The idea is that these toggles will allow less experienced, mentally fatigued, or disabled players to progress without too much friction.

Sources indicate that and just to be clear, enabling these settings does not disable Trophies. The bottom line here is that if you're having trouble getting through GTA 6, these options should almost certainly help.

Speaking of help, you can check out our overall GTA 6 guide and our totally spoiler-free Tips & Tricks guide for assistance with everything from collectibles to neat gameplay features you may not know about.

Sources indicate that as for the other accessibility settings on offer, Rockstar's covered a lot of ground. For starters, there are a bunch of aim assist and lock on options, while button taps and presses can be customised to an impressive extent, to make them less physically demanding.

You can even toggle "simplified" minigames, making the controls less complex, and there are multiple ways to customise controller layouts.

On top of that, a multitude of low vision options are available, there's a one-toggle brightness modifier, and there's a dedicated high contrast setting. Again, it's good stuff from the developer.

According to recent reports, have you been adjusting any of these options for your playthrough of GTA 6? Are you happy to see Rockstar adopting a more accessible approach? Snap to your target in the comments section below.

Upsettingly, it is that time of the week again, as Take-Two are laying off staff at Firaxis, the developer behind Civilization and XCOM, only a little over a year the last time the studio suffered from layoffs. Firaxis are, notably, owned by Take-Two, the publisher of GTA 6 which comes out in, oh, two days time? Interesting timing, 'ey.

It has been revealed that word of the layoffs came from Bloomberg, who report that about 60 people are losing their jobs, apparently roughly a third of its staff. The studio's head, Heather Hazen, is also leaving. A spokesperson for 2K Games (the Take-Two label that manages Firaxis) shared a statement on the layoffs: "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years.

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis." I don't feel personally confident in the idea that the only way to make a company succeed is by laying a bunch of people off thereby making it much harder to make anything in the first place, especially in the lead-up to what will likely be the best selling game of the decade, but what do I know!

Sources indicate that bloomberg also report Firaxis have been working on a newly introduced XCOM, which is yet to be announced, but the project has apparently had to contend with numerous development complications, missing a "significant milestone over the summer." This new XCOM game hasn't been cancelled at the very least, but anonymous sources that spoke with Bloomberg remarked it may have to deal with a shakeup due to the cuts. As always, solidarity with all those affected by this situation.

  • "After approximately 20 years, I was sadly one of those affected by recent layoffs," he noted in his posts.
  • On Twitter/X, he quote tweeted a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch and featuring footage from many of the games he worked on to share his message.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that treyarch's former Senior lead writer, Craig Houston, has been laid off after approximately 20 years of service with the developer. In a post made to both his Twitter/X account and LinkedIn, the developer thanked fans for their support during his two decades with the company and confirmed he was impacted by recent reorganistation within the studio.

"After approximately 20 years, I was sadly one of those affected by recent layoffs," he noted in his posts. "I am proud to have worked with so many talented people - many of whom will remain friends for life. Thanks to all the fans for your enthusiasm, support, and kind words over the years.".

On Twitter/X, he quote tweeted a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch and featuring footage from many of the games he worked on to share his message. It appears the layoffs referenced are part of the broad reorganistation affecting 3200 jobs that Xbox confirmed earlier this year. Treyarch, as part of Activision Blizzard, is owned by Xbox.

Industry observers note that houston is a bonafide veteran of the esteemed FPS series. His first Call of Duty title at Treyarch was Call of Duty 3, where he worked as a video editor. This was followed by World at War, Black Ops 1 through 4, where he is credited as a writer and designer. For Modern Warfare, Black Ops - Cold War, Vanguard, Modern Warfare 3, then Black Ops 6 and 7, he is listed as a member of the design team and in 'creative development'. He is not credited on this year's Modern Warfare 4.

If you've picked up a Call of Duty game in the past decade-plus, you'll have interacted with Houston's work: he was a central creative force behind the writing for Treyarch's campaign modes since 2006 (with Call of Duty 3) and the main writer for the Zombies mode since 2008 (with Call of Duty: World at War). Alongside Jimmy Zielinski, Jason Blundell, and Kevin Drew, Houston was an integral part of the evolution of the Zombies pillar of Call of Duty, and shaped it into the series-defining thing it is today. There has been a fair amount of community support for Houston since he announced the news yesterday; he was a popular dev, and a lot of the Zombies-specific fan communities online hold a lot of respect for him.

Industry observers note that "Craig is a great guy," notes one user on Reddit. "You can tell how much he loves the story/characters he writes just by how excited he is when he talks about them in promo material.".

Recent findings suggest that "You're a Legend Craig, it was an honor to work with you," indicates ex-Treyarch vet, Tony Flame, in a reply to Houston's X post. "You created a truly special experience that will live on in the kinds of millions fans. Wishing you the best [...].".

From all of us here at Eurogamer, and myself personally - who really admires the character-work and emergent storytelling present in the Xbox 360-era Call of Duty games, specifically - we wish you the best and good luck with the future, Craig.

With the pricing of memory right now, it's hard to get too excited for gaming handhelds, but Lenovo's reportedly more budget-friendly Legion Go Beam does intrigue me. And, with a recent leak, I'm now looking forward to hearing about the full details in the fresh year.

Recent findings suggest that this leak comes courtesy of Windows Latest, which managed to get its hands on three images, plus the name, and a suggestion that it will be less expensive than the Legion Go 2. Admittedly, the Legion Go 2 and its OLED screen are climbing up to $2,000 right now, so undercutting that isn't super tough.

The Go Beam has a white shell with lime green accents at the bottom, on the face buttons, around the thumbsticks, and on the start and menu buttons. It's a striking theme, even if I fear grubby fingers will make that white far grimmer in a matter of months.

There is, unfortunately, a lot we don't know about this handheld. We don't know the screen's panel technology; we don't know what size and weight it is; we don't know what processor powers it; we don't have a price point, and we don't yet have a release date.

Windows Latest is guessing it will be cheaper than the Legion Go based on its feature set, which is not a bad call.

Industry observers note that you get most of the controls you expect from a modern handheld, with triggers and bumpers, as well as two paddles on the back. There's a single USB Type-C port on the top of the device, and it has a sequence of eight fan holes in the back left.

It is, however, missing the small touchpad under the right thumbstick that comes with the Lenovo Legion Go S (both Windows and SteamOS models). That means navigating the desktop UI could be a little less easy, though at launch it wasn't usable in SteamOS anyways. It also has bigger bezels than the Go 2 and Go S.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products.

In a recent development, lenovo has been very fond of AMD with its gaming handhelds thus far, using Ryzen Z2, Z2 Extreme and Ryzen Z2 Go chips, but there is a suggestion the Beam could be kitted with a lower-end Panther Lake chip (perhaps the Intel Arc G3 and its Arc B370 iGPU). I haven't spent much time with the G3, but I have been very impressed with the G3 Extreme, from both a performance and battery life perspective.

It has been revealed that with Lenovo attending CES at the start of 2027, Windows Latest reckons that is when we will see more about this handheld. But it does note that Lenovo doesn't mention gaming for the January show, so it could be holding out for later in 2027, perhaps Computex in June.

Either way, if Lenovo is putting out cheaper handhelds, that's certainly not bad news for us PC gamers, even if we're still going to be paying an arm and a leg for the memory and storage inside it.
